titleText.es: Al final se funda la ONU. Y luego un rebelde solitario arría toda la fila de banderas de delante de la fachada, corre hasta su base, y consigue tropecientos millones de puntos.
titleText.en: Eventually a UN is set up. And then a lone rebel runs down the line of flags in front of it, runs back to his base, and gets a kajillion points.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive translates the capture-the-flag continuation freely: it explicitly says that the rebel lowers the whole row of flags and uses the playful number tropecientos millones for the enormous score.

regions.labelEs: HACE TRES AÑOS, EL REINO DE LIATE DERROCÓ SU ANTIGUO ORDEN Y ESTABLECIÓ UNA MONARQUÍA CONSTITUCIONAL. NUESTROS LÍDERES FIRMARON UN TRATADO CON SU REINA, Y NUESTRAS FRONTERAS QUEDARON ESTABLECIDAS POR LOS ACUERDOS DE YARBIS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Liate is the unchanged invented kingdom name rather than a Spanish lexical word.
Yarbis is the unchanged invented name of the accords rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Hace comes before the amount tres años to place the event three years before the present.
The noun monarquía comes first and constitucional follows it as the description.
Constitucional is singular to match monarquía and has the same singular form with either gender.
Derrocó presents the overthrow as one completed historical event.
Estableció presents the creation of the new system as a completed event.
Firmaron presents the treaty signing as a completed event by several people.
Quedaron presents the setting of the borders as a completed historical result.
Fronteras names the things, quedaron introduces the resulting state, and establecidas describes that state with a feminine plural ending.
Establecidas has the feminine plural ending -as to match fronteras.

regions.labelEs: MUCHOS DECÍAN QUE LA GUERRA NO TENDRÍA FIN, QUE LA PAZ SIEMPRE SERÍA UN SUEÑO APLAZADO.

applications.explanationEn: Decían presents what many people kept saying as background rather than one bounded statement.
No negates the prediction, tendría is tener's ‘would have’ form, and fin names the absent end.
Ser keeps its full dictionary form and takes -ía to express ‘would be.’
The noun sueño comes first and aplazado follows it as the description.
Aplazado is masculine singular to match sueño.

regions.labelEs: PERO HOY NUESTRA BANDERA ONDEA ORGULLOSA SOBRE NUESTRA EMBAJADA EN SU REINO, Y ELLOS PUEDEN CAMINAR POR NUESTRAS TIERRAS SIN TEMOR ALGUNO.

applications.explanationEn: Orgullosa has a feminine singular ending because it describes bandera, even though the verb stands between them.
Pueden matches the plural subject, and caminar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Sin creates the negative setting, temor names what is absent, and post-noun alguno strengthens the meaning to ‘any fear at all.’

regions.labelEs: VEN, VIAJERO. ABANDONA TUS RENCORES Y REÚNETE CON NOSOTROS EN HERMANDAD. ES HORA NO DE LUCHAR, SINO DE VIVIR.

applications.explanationEn: Ven is the irregular positive command telling one familiar person to come.
Abandona is the positive command telling one familiar person to leave something behind.
Reúnete is a positive command addressed to one familiar person.
The short pronoun te attaches to the end of the positive command reúne, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Reúnete is the command form with te attached, con is required before the other party, and nosotros names that group.

applications.exampleEs: ES HORA NO DE LUCHAR, SINO DE VIVIR
applications.explanationEn: Es hora frames the moment to act; each de introduces one unchanged action verb, while the surrounding contrast rejects luchar and selects vivir.

applications.exampleEs: NO DE LUCHAR, SINO DE VIVIR
applications.explanationEn: No rejects the first de plus action, and sino introduces the replacement with the required de repeated.

regions.labelEs: ESTE ES EL PEOR SERVIDOR DE CAPTURE-THE-FLAG DE LA HISTORIA.

excludedUnits.rationale: The game-mode name remains printed in English rather than being Spanish lexical text.

applications.exampleEs: EL PEOR SERVIDOR DE CAPTURE-THE-FLAG DE LA HISTORIA
applications.explanationEn: El and peor mark servidor as the lowest-ranked member of the group, while de la historia sets all of history as the comparison range—natural English can express this as ‘ever.’

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.
Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.promptEs: banderas · fronteras · servidor de capturar la bandera
cards.questionEn: Why does the final complaint reinterpret the diplomatic speech?
cards.answerEn: Capture the flag is a team game in which players enter opposing territory, take a flag, and return it to their base. The solemn kingdoms, borders, embassies, flags, and peace appeal are revealed as role-play on a badly designed game server.
cards.noteEn: The title text continues the game logic with a rebel collecting a row of flags and returning to base for an enormous score.
Derrocó is a completed-past form for one person, group, or state.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Su does not show the owner's gender. Here a singular institution or place is the owner.
Before a noun, antiguo often means former or previous rather than physically old.

cards.answerEn: order; established social or political system
cards.noteEn: Orden is masculine when it means an arrangement, command, or established system.

example.es: El cambio alteró el orden político.
example.en: The change altered the political order.

cards.noteEn: Estableció is a completed-past form for one person, group, or institution.

example.es: El país estableció un nuevo sistema.
example.en: The country established a new system.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Constitucional has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.
Firmaron is firmar's completed-past form for more than one person.
Here tratado is a noun naming an agreement between governments, not the completed form of tratar.

example.es: Los dos países aprobaron el tratado.
example.en: The two countries approved the treaty.

cards.noteEn: Su stays singular because the possessed thing is singular, even when the owners are several people. Sus is used before a plural possessed thing.

cards.promptEs: cosa + quedar + participio que describe el resultado
cards.questionEn: How can quedar describe the state left by a completed action?
cards.answerEn: Name the thing, use the matching form of quedar, and add the completed-action form with an ending that matches the thing.
cards.noteEn: For example, la puerta quedó cerrada and las reglas quedaron establecidas describe the resulting states of the door and rules.

cards.answerEn: were left; ended up (in a resulting state)
cards.noteEn: A form of quedar can introduce the state that remains after an event. The following completed-action form describes that state.
The -as ending matches more than one feminine thing being described.
In a diplomatic context, acuerdos can name formal agreements between governments.

cards.answerEn: they said; they used to say
cards.noteEn: Decían is an imperfect-past form for repeated, ongoing, or background speech by more than one person.

example.en: Many people used to say it was impossible.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has no end?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a matching form of tener, and fin.
cards.noteEn: The form of tener changes with the subject and time: no tiene fin, no tendría fin, no tuvo fin.

example.es: La espera parecía no tener fin.

cards.noteEn: To make this ‘would’ form, tener changes to the irregular base tendr- and adds -ía. The following noun states what would be had.

example.es: El proyecto tendría un coste alto.
example.en: The project would have a high cost.

cards.noteEn: Sería is the “would” form of ser, “to be.” Spanish keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía.

example.en: It would be a good solution.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.
Aplazado describes something moved to a later time.
Ondea is a present-time form for one flag or other thing moving in waves.

example.es: La bandera ondea sobre el edificio.
example.en: The flag flies over the building.

cards.noteEn: Orgullosa matches a feminine singular thing. With a verb of movement or appearance, English may express the same idea with an adverb such as proudly.
Sobre can introduce the geographical area across which something is measured or happens. This is different from sobre meaning ‘about’ a topic.

example.es: La tormenta avanza sobre la costa.
example.en: The storm moves over the coast.

cards.noteEn: Here ellos is the subject that performs the following action.

cards.answerEn: they can; they are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.
In a political or geographic context, tierras can mean a people's territory rather than separate pieces of soil.

cards.questionEn: How can alguno or alguna strengthen a negative after a noun?
cards.answerEn: Use the negative word first, then the noun, and put alguno or alguna after that noun.
cards.noteEn: This formal or emphatic order means ‘any ... at all’: sin temor alguno, no existe razón alguna.

example.en: He showed no interest at all.

cards.answerEn: any; at all (after a noun in a negative setting)
cards.noteEn: Alguno normally means some before a noun. After a noun and following a negative word such as sin, it strengthens the negative meaning.

example.en: She did it without any problem at all.

cards.noteEn: Ven is the irregular positive command of venir, ‘to come,’ for tú, the familiar singular ‘you.’

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Abandona tells one familiar person to leave something behind.
Reunirse uses reúne for the positive command to one familiar person, and te is attached at the end because the action is joining or meeting with others. The written accent preserves the stress.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?
How do you say that someone meets up with or joins another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of reunirse followed by con and the person or group.
cards.noteEn: The short pronoun changes with the subject: me reúno, te reúnes, se reúne, nos reunimos. In a positive command it attaches to the end: reúnete.

example.en: We met up with the team.

cards.answerEn: it is (in an impersonal time expression)
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use es without a separate subject word in expressions such as es hora, “it is time.” English supplies the impersonal word “it.”

cards.promptEs: es hora de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that it is time to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use es hora de, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Negation and contrast can surround the action: es hora no de discutir, sino de decidir.
After es, hora can identify the appropriate moment for an action rather than a clock hour.

cards.promptEs: no + opción A, sino + opción B
cards.questionEn: How do you reject one option and replace it with another?
cards.answerEn: Put no before the rejected option and sino before its replacement.
cards.noteEn: Repeat a required preposition when both options need it: no de correr, sino de caminar.

example.en: We are not looking for excuses, but rather solutions.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links es hora to the action whose time has come
cards.noteEn: After es hora, use de before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
After a negative statement, sino replaces the rejected option with a contrasting one.

example.en: I do not want to run, but rather to walk.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that something is the best or worst ever?
cards.answerEn: Use a highest-or-lowest form such as el mejor, el peor, or el más largo, then add de la historia.
cards.noteEn: A highest-or-lowest form is called a superlative. De la historia sets all of history as its comparison range; natural English often uses ‘ever’ or ‘in history.’

example.es: Fue el partido más largo de la historia.
example.en: It was the longest game ever.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, los, or las, peor normally means “worst.” Without an article it often means “worse.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

cards.answerEn: in; among (introducing what ‘best’ or ‘worst’ is compared across)
cards.noteEn: After a highest-or-lowest description such as el mejor or el peor, de can introduce the full group or time range being compared.

example.es: Es la mejor canción de la década.
example.en: It is the best song of the decade.
